To our visitors

A note from Joseph

For more than twenty years I have worked across finance, microfinance and startups. I have seen capital help a company grow a second growth curve, and I have seen a single small loan change a family's everyday life.

I believe capital can deliver both returns and good. If you are thinking about your company's next step, the direction of your family's capital, or a startup that deserves support, I would be glad to sit down and talk.

— Joseph

About

As Vice Chairman of Anue Securities Investment Consulting and General Manager of Anue (cnYes), I built Anue Fund into Taiwan's largest independent online fund platform within four years, with more than US$1.5 billion in assets, and led the group's transformation from financial media into a regulated financial services group.

Before that I led an online lending and investment platform that completed nearly US$28 billion in lending and crowdfunding transactions within 24 months. Earlier, as Senior Vice President at Temasek-owned Fullerton Financial Holdings, I was seconded to Alibaba Group to co-develop financial services, then served as Regional General Manager for North and Southwest China, running SME and supply-chain finance and supporting the sale of the business to Ping An Group. Before that, as Greater China COO of Opportunity International, I built and managed rural microfinance and credit guarantee companies. I began my career at Mastercard and Deloitte Consulting.

Education: MBA, Graduate Institute of Business Administration, National Taiwan University; BS in Mathematics, National Taiwan University; Electronics, Hsin Pu Junior College of Technology.

Record Growth, But Not for Most of Taiwan

As resources flow to semiconductors, who will invest in education, the environment, the humanities and the next generation of startups?

Taiwan's economy grew 13.72% in the first half, but growth is concentrated in electronics and ICT. Concentration is happening across markets as well as industries, and education, social welfare, the environment and the humanities lack suitable capital tools rather than attention. Experience abroad shows that patient capital, willing to wait and take early risk, is what fills these gaps, and Taiwan's family businesses, corporates, financial institutions and public funds are well placed to provide it.

2026.10.4Family officesImpact investing

If a Family Only Brings Money, It Brings the Most Replaceable Thing

From 'special assets' to additionality: the unique role of family capital in impact investing

What families truly pass on are special assets that markets cannot supply, which is exactly how impact investing defines additionality. This piece answers the three questions families care about most: returns, governance and the next generation, and explains how impact investing can hold a family's shared purpose once control is let go.

2026.10.4Impact investingFamily officesCatalytic capital

Money Willing to Wait Ten Years Is the Scarcest Capital in the Market

Catalytic capital is not the same as sacrifice: from the Rhino Bond to Singapore's family office incentives

Catalytic capital is not the same as first loss. Using the anchor tenant of a shopping mall as an analogy, this piece lays out catalytic capital as a four-rung ladder from cheapest to most expensive, argues that what families can most easily offer, and most often undervalue, is time, and draws on the World Bank's Rhino Bond and Singapore's blended finance incentives for family offices to show how those who go first need not lose out.

2026.10.4Family officesImpact investingPolicy

Asia's New Family Office Race Isn't About Tax Rates

From Hong Kong and Singapore to Japan: how regulators are building impact into the rules for family wealth

Hong Kong sets direction through research, Singapore lowers costs through incentives, and Japan builds a shared language through a national platform. Competition among Asia's financial centers is shifting from tax rates and thresholds to whose capital can prove what it created.

ImpactAlpha2026-10-07

Family office Ceniarth reveals break-even results from its impact-first portfolio

Ceniarth, an $800m family office, has deployed over $300m of impact-first capital across about 90 funds and 60 direct deals. Its four-year net IRR was 3.2%, roughly zero after costs and inflation; breaking even needs about 4.5% gross. Rare, candid data for families sizing impact allocations.

MacArthur Foundation2026-10-08

MacArthur Foundation lifts its impact investment pool 50% to $750 million

The MacArthur Foundation is raising its impact investment allocation by 50% to $750m, starting in 2027, with repaid capital redeployed into new deals. It also extended its pledge to pay out at least 6% through 2028. A major foundation scaling up signals impact investing is now a core philanthropic tool.
